claims.claim: SELECT audit_log_filter_set_user('%', 'conn_ddl');           -- default for all accounts
claims.evidence_quote: On connect, the component loads one filter definition from the matching USER / HOST row in mysql.audit_log_user , or falls back to the default account ( % ).
claims.note: Confirms the '%' default: an account with no matching USER/HOST row falls back to the default account; the same page adds 'A concrete account (for example admin @ localhost) overrides a % assignment', and the blocked MySQL filtering page states 'The filter assigned to % is used for connections from any account that has no explicitly assigned filter (which initially is true for all accounts)'.

Source page blocked to the checker (see coverage), read via the web fetch tool today. The MySQL filtering page states: 'To log all auditable events for all users, use the following statements, which create a simple filter to enable logging and assign it to the default account: SELECT audit_log_filter_set_filter('log_all', '{ "filter": { "log": true } }'); SELECT audit_log_filter_set_user('%', 'log_all');' and, for per-account assignment, 'To assign a filter explicitly to a particular user account or accounts, define the filter, then assign it to the relevant accounts' - 'Now full logging is enabled for user1@localhost and user2@localhost.'

claims.claim: SELECT * FROM mysql.audit_log_filter; SELECT * FROM mysql.audit_log_user;
claims.evidence_quote: The Audit Log Filter component uses mysql system tables on InnoDB . They hold account assignments and filter JSON.
claims.note: The same page lists both tables - 'The audit_log_filter table stores named filter definitions' (columns NAME and FILTER) and 'The audit_log_user table maps accounts to filters' (columns USER, HOST and FILTERNAME) - and the blocked MySQL filtering page adds that 'you can display audit filters by querying the mysql.audit_log_filter table'.
